name: sorted input breaks a BST
hook: Feed a binary search tree sorted data and it quietly becomes a linked list.
hook_slide: Feed a BST sorted data and it becomes *a linked list*.
hook_sub: Every promise still true. All of them worthless.
caption: Every BST operation costs O(h), where h is the tree's height. That's only fast if the tree's shape cooperates.
Insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order: every insert turns right, and you get {small_levels} levels for {small_levels} keys. Finding 5 visits all {small_visits} nodes.
At {n} sorted keys: {chain_levels} levels, {chain_visits} nodes visited to find the largest. Build the same keys middle-first and it's {balanced_levels} levels.
And sorted input isn't exotic: ordered files, timestamps, an already-sorted array. That's why real libraries don't hope for balance. They restore it with rotations.
Which self-balancing tree did you learn first? 👇
cta: What balanced means, and the one rotation that restores it.

p: h is the height, and it is only small if the tree's shape cooperates.
A *balanced* tree guarantees h = O(log n). No binary tree can be shorter than about log₂ n.
Every insert turns right, because every value is larger than everything already there. The tree collapses into a straight line.
Nothing here is wrong. The shape comes from the order of the input.
Data loaded from an ordered file, timestamps arriving in order, an already-sorted array inserted one element at a time.
So real libraries don't hope for balance. They restore it as the tree changes, *with rotations*.
